div.p: Graphical Communicating Shared Resources is a formal language ,for the specification and analysis of real-time systems, including their functional, temporal and resource repuiremenlis. GCSR supports the explicit representation of syslem resources and priorities to arbitrate resource contentions. These features allow a designer to examine resource inherent constraints and to experiment with various resource allo- cations and scheduling disciplines in order to produce a more dependable specification. In addition, GCSR has a precise operational semantics and notions of equivalence that nllow the execution and formal analysis of a specification. In this paper, we show how to model a scheduling discipline and verify schedulability and safety properties within GCSR. We illustrate our method through 0: mobile rohotic application.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The Communicating Shared Resources (CSR) paradigm is an ongoing project at the University of Pennsylvania to build a formal framework for the development of real-time systems. It is based on the premise that the timed behavior of a real-time system is affected not only by the time its components take to execute and synchronize, but also by delays introduced due to the scheduling of actions that compete for shared resources. One of the objectives of the CSR paradigm is therefore to provide a rigorous framework in which the run-time resource requirements of a realtime system can be specified together with its functional requirements. The integration of the two types of system requirements has several advantages. One advantage is that designers can formally specify and rigorously analyze and test various design alternatives before implementation. Another is that designers can consider resource-induced constraints during the de-*This research w,as supported in part by NSF CCR-9311622, NSF CCR-9415346, AFOSR F49620-95-1-0508, ARO DAAH04-95-1-0092, and NSF SBR 8920230.
sign stage of the development cycle; this in turn allows them to develop more realistic design solutions.

Within the CSR paradigm, we developed the Graphical Communicating Shared Resources (GCSR) [l] for the following reasons. One reason is that, similar to most other formal methods, the CSR formalisms developed so far (CCSR [6] and ACSR [9,21) tend to be not easily accessible to practitioners, in part, because of their mathematical, textual notations that often produce obtuse specifications. Another reason is that popular graphical languages for real-time sys- tems (Statecharts [7], Modechart [8 and Communicating Real-time State Machines [13h do not support explicit notions of resources. While it might be possible to encode the run-time resource requirements as boolean conditions using formalisms without explicit notions of resources, the resulting specification is often complex and hard to modify. (For an example, the reader is referred to the description of the Modechart toolset MT [5] where several tasks of a missile system are modeled together with a CPU allocation.)

In addition, the development of the GCSR language is motivated by two other concerns: one is to support the modular, hierarchical, and thus, scalable specification of real-time systems; the other is to benefit from the analysis techniques [3, 101 and toolset [4] develolped for the Algebra of Communicating Shared Resources ACSR), timed process algebra that is devel-Statecharts and Modechart support modularity through their notions of state and mode, respectively; they, however, lack a notion of scopes for variables since they allow a variable to be used in any state and mode. Furthermore, Statecharts and Modechart support hierarchy through state and mode nesting, but allow edges to cross state and mode boundaries. Such a feature can be compared to goto statements in high-level programming languages as it may create unstructured specifications. Also, there are graphical ambiguities in describing when control moves out of a state and mode: does control abort the execution of oped wit 6 in the CSR paradigm. the source mode, or does it wait for its completion? GCSR remedies these weaknesses by offering several types of nodes and edges. In GCSR, the visibility scope of communication events, which reflect potential dependencies between nodes, can be limited. Furthermore, GCSR disallows edges from crossing node boundaries and offers instead two types of edges that graphically distinguish between control transfer due to an interrupt versus an exception, i.e., involuntary versus voluntary release of control.

The semantics of GCSR can be defined either directly as a labeled transition system or through a translation to the ACSR process algebra. As shown in [l], the second way of defining the semantics of GCSR allows a designer t o interchangeably use the graphical and textual notations, for example, to specify the high-level view of a system graphically and fill the details of components textually. In addition, since we already have developed VERSA [4], a toolset for the specification, syntactic manipulation, execution, and equivalence checking of ACSR specifications, we can use VERSA to analyze GCSR specifications by an automated translation from GCSR to ACSR. We have extended VERSA with a graphical user interface that allows the drawing, syntactic checking, and automated translation of GCSR specifications.

In this paper, we describe the GCSR language and illustrate how the explicit representation of resources and priorities allows a designer to model static priority based scheduling disciplines and to experiment with different resource allocations without major changes to a given design solution. We use a robotic application to illustrate schedulability and safety analysis in GCSR. The analysis is based on verifying deadlock freeness.

div.head: Mobile Robot
div.p: The system consists of a robot that autonomously navigate in an environment while avoiding obstacles. The robot is equipped with sensors, e.g., cameras, to monitor the environment and actuators to react upon detecting an obstacle by rotating a set of wheels to move the robot. The robot also has two dedicated processors, cpul and cpu2, to process collected sensory data and to determine and execute navigation strategies.

The software architecture, which is inherited from the system functionality, consists of three components: an obstacle detection and avoidance planning strategy, a normal motion planning strategy, and a motion execution strategy. The obstacle detection and avoidance planning strategy is a periodic task with period d l and computation time e l . The normal motion planner is also a periodic task with period d2 > d l and computation time c2. The motion execution strategy synchronizes its computation with the other two components through two communication events: obs when an obstacle is detected, and loc when a safe, target location to which the robot must move is set.

Since there are three tasks and only two processors, it is obvious that the behavior of the system will depend on the resource allocation scheme and how resource contention is resolved. A design solu-tion that explicitly incorporates these decisions gives the designer more confidence in the solution before the implementation stage. We will use the above mobile robotic example to illustrate how we can model it in GCSR to describe the behavior of the system, the resource allocation, as well as resolution of resource contention through priorities. In addition, we will show how to verify the safety of a design and the schedulability of tasks that share a processor under a specific scheduling discipline.

div.head: The GCSR Language
div.p: The GCSR paradigm is based on the view that a real-time system consists of a set of communicating components, called processes, that execute on a finite set of serially reusable resources and synchronize with one another through communication channels. The use of shared resources is represented by timed ac- tions, and synchronization is supported by instantaneous events. The execution of an action is assumed to take nonzero time units with respect to a global clock, and to consume a set of resources during that time. The execution of an action is subject to the availability of the resources it uses. Contention for resources is arbitrated according to the priorities of competing actions. To ensure uniform progress of time, processes execute actions synchronously. Time can be either dense or discrete. However, for implementation reasons, we consider discrete time only.

Unlike an action, the execution of an event is instantaneous and never consumes any resource. Processes execute events asynchronously except when two processes synchronize through matching event names, i.e., channels.

Graphically, a GCSR process is represented by a finite set of nodes that are connected with directed edges. Figures 2 and3 show the graphical GCSR symbols. Before describing the details of these symbols, we first use the motion executor component of the mobile robot to illustrate the GCSR symbols. ior of the process MotEzec is as follows. When control enters the initial node of MotExec, the process starts behaving like the process Wait. The Wait recursively consumes time andl no resources. Within the process MotExec, the execution of the Wait process can be interrupted in two ways which correspond to the event-labeled edges out of the node Wait: one is by receiving the event (obs?, 2) and another by receiving the event (loc?, 1). Receiving the event obs has a higher priority than receiving the event loc. This reflects the fact that avoiding isn obstacle is more critical than normal motion.

div.p: Once the event (obs?, 2) is received, control instantaneously moves to the target node of the edge. In this node, control remains for t o time units while using the cpul resource at priority level po. This node represents the robot avoiding an obstacle detected in its environment. After t o time units, control moves back to the initial node where the robot is ready to execute a navigation strategy.

If event (loc'?, 1) is received, while the event ( o h ? , 2) was not present, control instantaneously moves to the target node of the corresponding eventlabeled edge. This node is a compound node where the nested GCSR process represents the navigation strategy in the absence of obstacles. Control starts at the initial node of the nested process which is an instantaneous node. At this nodle, an instantaneous deci- sion must be made whether to idle or use the cpul resource at priority level pur. .As we will see in Section 4, the choice between the two actions is determined by the availability of the cpul resource. The execution of the nested process can be stopped in three ways: the first way is by the reception of the event ( o h ? , 2) at which time control moves to the node where the avoidance strategy is executed; the second way is by a timeout after control has remained tu, time units inside the compound node; and the third way is when the nested process relinquishes control by sending the event (done!, 1) at which time control moves through the edge labeled with (done?,l) back to the initial node of the MotExec process. The first two types of control transfer do not depend on the nested process; the third on the other hand is initiated by the nested process itself.

div.head: GCSR Nodes and Edges
div.p: Figure 2 shows the graphical symbols for the five types of GCSR nodes.

The Resource attribute of a time-consuming node is a set of (resource, priority) pairs, with the restriction that each resource is listed once. The Name attribute of a reference node refers to the name of a GCSR process. The Restrict and Close attributes of a compound node are sets of event names and resource names, respectively.

The motivation for various node symbols in GCSR is a succinct and scalable r,epresentation of the different system activities and components. The instantaneous node requires that no delay is allowed before the next activity. In contrast, the time-consuming node describes a time consuming action. Furthermore, the Resource attribute of a time-consuming node explicitly describes the required resources for the system action and makes it easy to modify any resource re-quirement to reflect different resource allocation and scheduling disciplines. The nil node describes a halting process, i.e., end of system execution. The reference node allows the decomposition of a large specification into subspecifications which eases the visual structuring of such a specification. On the other hand, the compound node visually distinguishes a system action from a system component. It is essential in supporting scalable and modular specifications since it allows a designer to 1 group GCSR processes into a higher level entity, 2) connect several GCSR processes that are executed sequentially, and 3) reflect the fact that system components execute in parallel. In addition to the structural modularity, compound nodes also provide for semantic modularity by encapsulating dependencies through their Restrict and Close attributes. The Restrict attribute identifies a set of events that are local to the GCSR nested processes inside the node; they are not visible outside the node boundaries. The Close attribute identifies a set of resources that are reserved for the nested GCSR processes, even if their actions do not explicitly request them.

GCSR nodes can be connected with edges to describe sequential execution. GCSR offers four types of edges shown in Figure 3. The distinct symbols for exception edges and the other edges are motivated by the dlesire to support a structured, hierarchical specification in which edges do not cross node boundaries and to graphically distinguish two types of control flow: one that is externally controlled by an interacting process and one that is triggered internally through voluntary release of control by raising an exception. The second type of control flow is specified using an exception edge. Control moves to the destination node of a m exception edge when the process at the source node executes an exception event that labels the exception edge. The transfer of control through an exception edge allows synchronization between a process inside a compound node with an outside node and thus emulates a transition between nodes at different levels of nesting.
The circle node is any node.

div.head: Informal Semantics
div.p: Intuitively, the behavior of a GCSR process consists of a sequence of execution steps each of which represents either a communication event or a time and resource consuming action. For example, in Figure 4 (a), once execution reaches the instantaneous node, the system sends the event named e at priority 1 and then execution moves instantaneously to the target node of the event-labeled edge from where execution continues. On the other hand, in Figure 4 (b) execution remains in the time-consuming node for 3 time units while using simultaneously the cup1 resource at priority level 1 and the cup2 resource at priority level 2; after three time units in the source node, execution moves to the target node of the time-labeled edge.

In addition to this basic notion of sequential execution in GCSR, several processes can be combined through compound nodes to describe a large system where processes execute in sequence or in parallel. For example, in Figure 5 (a), once execution reaches the compound node, the GCSR process P is executed for at most t time units, after which execution moves to the target node of the time-labeled edge. The execution of P can also be terminated in two other ways. One way is when the target node of the unlabeled edge is enabled, the execution of P is aborted and execution moves to the target node. Another way of terminating the execution of P is through an exception raised by P which sends the event a. At this time, the execution moves to the target node of the exception edge, labeled with the receive event a at priority p . The dif-ference is that, in the former the enabling of the edge is caused by a process other than P , whereas in the latter the enabling of the edge is caused by the process

GCSR processes can also be combined in parallel by nesting them inside a compound node. When control reaches a compound node, it simultaneously enters all the initial nodes of its nested GCSR processes. Control can move through event-labeled edges in different nested processes in an interleaved fashion for unrestricted events, but synchronously in any two nested processes for restricted events. In addition, if control spends time in one nested process, then control in all the remaining nested processes must be in timeconsuming nodes where it can spend time. This forces synchronous time passage between parallel processes. Furthermore, since resources are assumed to be serial, the set of resources used in all the time-consuming nodes that simultaneously have control must be disjoint. For example, in Figure 5 (b) the processes P1 and P2 execute in parallel. Furthermore, P1 and P2 communicate privately through the event named s and use the resource T exclusively; that is, if the compound node is combined in parallel with another GCSR process, this latter can not communicate with P1 and P2 through the event s and will not have access to the resource r unless it requires it at a higher priority.

The overall behavior of a GCSR process can be formally described as a labeled transition system where each transition represents an execution step with the label being a communication event or a time and resource consuming action. In the translation of a GCSR process to a labeled transition system, there are two main difficulties that stem from handling the time-labeled edges and the unlabeled edges. The timelabeled edges require a notion of local clock associated with each time-labeled edge to keep track of how long control remained inside the source node. The local clocks of edges in parallel components are decremented each time the global clock "ticks". When the local clock of an edge reaches zero, control moves to the source node of the edge. The unlabeled edges do not participate in a visible activity, i.e., communication event of time and resource consumption. We therefore had t o define the semantics at two levels: the first level basically prunes out the unlabeled edges and produces the sequential execution steps in a GCSR process; the second level uses the first level transitions to define the parallel execution and synchironization within a GCSR process.

As seen in the previous examples, there might be several execution steps that are simultaneously possible. The selection among such execution steps is done via a notion of priority. Informally, the selection among two execution steps that are simultaneously possible is either nondetermmistic, or is arbitrated according to the following three rules for selecting an execution step a over an execution step p: 1) a and ,f? are events with the same label and a has a higher priority; 2) a and p are actions and a uses a subset of the resources used in p at priorit,ies no lower than in p and with at least one resource in a at a higher priority; or 3). a is a r event (i.e., synchronization of two events) with a non-zero priority and p is a time-consuming action. (The technical reasons behind these rules are rather complicated and outside the scope of this pa-

The second way of defining the semantics of GCSR is through a translation to ACSR: each GCSR process is translated to an ACSR process. The translation is consistent with the direct semantics, in the sense that the corresponding ACSR process has an equivalent labeled transition to the one generated directly from the GCSR process. This direct translation which we have implemented in the GCSR toolset allowed us to use the ACSR toolset VERSA to execute and analyze GCSR specifications.

To define precisely the semantics of GCSR, either directly or through ACSR, we imposed syntactic restrictions on how edges can connect nodes. Detailed description of the syntax of well-defined GCSR processes and the CCSR-ACSR correspondence can be found in [ 11.

div.head: The Mobile Robot in GCSR
div.p: Figure 6 shows the high level structure of the mobile robot examlple in GCSR. In this first solution, the components in charge of planning motion strategies, ObstDetect and MotPlan, have been allocated on cpu2. The motion execution component, MotExec, is allocated on cpul.

Figure 7 shows the detailed specification of the MotExec process; this is at simplified version of the one in Figure 1. Figure 8 shows the detailed specifications of the ObstDeteci and MotPlan processes. Each of these lather processes consists of two processes that execute in parallel and coordinate their activities with the synchronization events start and end. The process ObsDetTaslc (Mot PlanTask represents the avoidance (normal motion planing) strategy. The second process ObsDestSchecl (MotPlanSched) serves as a dispatcher for the task: it instantiates the task by sending the event start and waits for its period to finish at which time it informs it to stop by sending the event end and instantiates it again for the following period. Note that at the end of the task period, the scheduler moves to an instantaneous node from which it can onlly send the event end; in particular it can not consume time. At this time, however, the task might not be able to receive the event end if it actual task that computes 1,he obstac 1 e detection and ---
is in any of its time-consuming nodes. By operational semantics of the parallel execution and event restriction, the system deadlocks at this instant, i.e., does not have any more execution steps.

Each of the two tasks, ObsDetTask and MotPlanTask, is modeled such that it waits for the event start, after which it can either acquire the cpu2 resource or idle. According to the preemption relation, acquiring the resource has a higher priority than idling. In addition, the task with the higher priority will acquire the cpu2 resource first. Once a task acquires the cpu2 resource, it executes without preemption until the end of its computation time. It then tries to signal the motion executor process the result of its computation (i.e., obs and loc, respectively) and waits for the event end to go back to the initial state of waiting.

Note that in the ObsDetTask process, after using the cpu2 resource for c l time units, the process can either send (06s!,2) or (danger!, 1). The first event when synchronized will have a higher priority. However, if the motion executor process is not ready to receive the obs event, the process will send the danger event, to indicate that an obstacle was detected but the motion planer is not aware of it and thus there is a potential safety violation: the robot may collide with the obstacle. We will use this event during the analysis stage in the next section to verify the safety of the system.

In the MotPlanTask process, the event loc is not as critical to send. This is modeled by the unlabeled edge which represents the possibility of skipping the synchronization with the motion executor on the event

div.p: Restrict={start,end} Close= Formal analysis and rigorous testing of a real-time specification before implementation is essential, especially for real-time systems that are embedded in safety critical applications. Analysis includes checkin that a design is valid with respect to a (requirements7 specification, and that a specification satisfies certain properties such as safety and schedulability of system processes, in the presence of resource sharing.

A real-time system property is usually expressed in terms of the (timed) occurrences of certain events. For example, a safety property can be formulated as "bad events never occur" or as "a bad event never occurs within t time units after some event ". In the presence of communication and resource sharing, deadlock freeness can be considered as a safety property. Furthermore, schedulability analysis in GCSR can be turned into verifying deadlock freeness; that is, a realtime system can be modeled such that if one process misses i)ts deadline, the system deadlocks [4].

The operational semantics of GCSR allows two types of analysis: execution to test a specification for "unintended" behaviors, and verification of properties through either state space exploration or behavioral equivalence checking. Within the CSR paradigm, there are two notions of behavioral equivalence that are defined over the prioritized labeled transition system. The first equivalence relation is based on strong bisimulation [12], w T , which ensures that equivalent processes match each other's execution steps, i.e., events and time-consuming actions. The second is based on weak bisimulation, M, , which ensures that equivalent processes match each other's execution steps for non-7 events but allows one process to make T execution steps that an equivalent process does not match. Based on the prioritized strong and weak bisimulations, we have defined two correspond-ing equivalence relations that abstract out certain resource names [lo]. These relations relate processes based on their behaviors while ignoring the usage of certain resources. It turns out that these equivalence relations are extremely useful since durin the specification phase, resource identity may not %e relevant, while it is important during the design phase.

In this paper, we use state space exploration to verify the safety and schedulability of a design and search for deadlocked states in the prioritized labeled transition system of the design. We note that an analysis based on state space exploration as well as equivinvolved have transition systems with a finite number of states. All of the processes we used in the mobile robot example are finite.

To verify the safety of our design, we proceed in two steps: we first build a simple, abstract tester process that basically either idles or synchronizes on the "bad" event and terminates, i.e., becomes the Nil process. We then run the tester process in parallel with the given design and force synchronization on all events. Figure 9 (a) shows the verification setting, where the * in the Restrict attribute indicates all events; Figure 9 ( b i shows a tester process for the safety of the mobile ro ot example where the event danger is the "bad" event. The semantics of the Parallel operator guarantees that the verification process SystemVeri f ier will reach a deadlocked state if and only $the Tester process enters its Nil node. In this case, we can conclude that the "bad" event in deed can happen and the design violates the safety property. We next verify the schedulability and safety of two design solutions for the mobile robot example. The first design uses the resource allocation of the previous section and the rate monotonic scheduling discipline [ll] to arbitrate the usage of the cpu2 resource between the ObstDetect and MotPlan processes. The second design shortens the period of the ObstDetect process and requires a diflerent resource allocation as we find out that the two processes are no longer schedulable on cpu2 under the rate monotonic scheduler. The second design illustrates the ease of changing resource requirements and priorities in GCSR.

VERSA supports a command that shows statistics about the transition system of a process, e.g., number of states, deadlocked states, and edges. Safety Analysis. The safety requirement for the mobile robot is that it does not collide into a detected obstacle. There are two potential ways to violate this safety requirement: one is when the motion planer does not execute the corresponding motion avoidance strategy and instead keeps on navigating; another is when the motion planer misses to receive the event obs from the obstacle detection process, ObstDetect.

In our design, the first scenario can be detected by the flow of control within the MotPlan process right after receiving the event (obs?, 2). It is straightforward to check that the first scenario does not happen. The second scenario can be detected by the occurrence of the event (danger!, 1) which is sent by the ObstDetect when it can not communicate with the MotPlan process right after finishing its computation.

To verify that the event danger never occurs in our design, we restricted the event danger in the SystemV eri f ier process of Figure 9; all other events in MobileRobot are already restricted. We then used the automated translation within the GCSR toolset to translate all the processes and used VERSA to verify that SystemVeri f ier has no deadlocked state, and thus, our MobileRobot design is safe.

div.p: To get a schedulable design, we relocate the ObstDetect process to cpuland move the M o t E x e c to the cpu2. The new architecture is show in Figure 10 (a). To reflect the new resource allocation in the detailed specifications of the components involved, we only need to change the Resource attributes of their time-consuming nodes. More specifically, the time consuming node of the O b s D e t T a s k process now has a Resource attribute of { ( c p u l , p l ) } and both timeconsuming nodes in the M o t E x e c process must have their cpul resource changed to cpu2.

With the new resource allocation, the system is however not safe any more: this is due to the fact that the M o t P l a n process may be running on the cpu2 resource when the Obst Detect process sends the event (obs!,Z) to the M o t E x e c process. This later can not preempt the M o t P l a n process which will have control in the time-consuming node with Resource attribute { ( c p u 2 , p 2 ) } . To fix the safety violation, there are two necessary changes: One is to make one of the processes preemptable; and the second is to adjust their priorities so that the most critical action is executed first.

Since the M o t E x e c process is an aperiodic process, we elected to make it preemptable. This requires to change the time-consuming action with the Resource attribute (cpu2,po) with a compound node where the nested process describe the behavior of either using the cpu2 resource or idling. Figure 10 (b) shows the modified process. Furthermore, to ensure preemption according to the importance of the actions, we assign priorities as follows: When the M o t E x e c process executes an obstacle avoidance strategy, it must run at the highest priority PO = 3; the MotPlan process executes at a lower priority p 2 = 2; and finally, when the M o t E x e c process executes normal navigation, it uses the processor at priority p w = 1. With this arbitration, the M o t P l a n process acquires the cpu2 resource if the M o t E x e c process does not need it to avoid an obstacle. It however can preempt the M o t E x e c process when executing a normal motion strategy. We used the automated GCSR to ACSR translation to verify that the new resource allocation and arbitration produces a safe design.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We have presented the Graphical Communicating Shared Resources (GCSR languages. The GCSR lanorities in an intuitive way tha.t produces easy to understand and modify specifications. These features allow a designer to incorporate resource requirements early in a development phase ancl experiment with different resource allocations to eliiminate unimplementable or undependable solutions. In addition, the GCSR operational semantics makes it possible to execute a GCSR specification and verilfy its correctness through state exploration and various notions of behavioral equivalence relations. We have illustrated how to conduct schedulability analysis and verify safety properties with GCSR through a mobile robot example. The analysis technique we used is based on detecting deadlocks.

One might argue that integrating too fine details about the resource requirements with the functional requirements of a real-time system might render the design process unwieldy. It would be therefore fruitful to develop a software engineering methodology where the resource requirements are added incrementally. The incremental integration of the resource requirements should preserve certain properties between different levels of design abstractions, e.g., deadlock freeness. We are currently working on a notion of refinement that will support such a notion of incremental specification of resource requirements. This notion of refinement also provides for a top-down and modular development of a GCSR specification. Here, a designer starts with an abstract, description that contains minimal details about the resource requirements, communications, and system components, which are represented as GCSR actions.
